text: Why does the JVM need `invokeinterface` when it already has `invokevirtual`?
choices: Interface methods are always public, and `invokevirtual` cannot express public dispatch.
Interfaces are loaded lazily, so their methods do not exist when `invokevirtual` resolves.
A class may implement any combination of interfaces, so no single method-table layout can give an interface method a fixed slot.
Interface methods may have `default` bodies, which `invokevirtual` cannot locate.
explanation: For classes, a subclass keeps the parent's table layout, so a slot number computed at compile time stays valid forever — including for subclasses written years later. Interfaces break that: if one class implements two interfaces, both cannot claim slot 0, and there is no layout that works for every combination. So the lookup must search, and call-site caching brings the measured cost back down.
